title: Futility of Futilities: Nothing New Under the Sun
summary: A narrator introduces the words of the Teacher, son of David and king in Jerusalem, and his motto: everything is futile. A poem follows on the endless cycles of generations, sun, wind, and rivers, where nothing is new and nothing is remembered. Then the Teacher speaks for himself, describing how he set out to explore everything done under heaven with wisdom and found it all to be a pursuit of the wind, and wisdom itself a source of grief.
story: Ecclesiastes stands among the Bible's wisdom books, after Proverbs, which taught that the wise and diligent generally prosper. This first chapter raises the question that will drive the whole book: “What does a man gain from all his labor, at which he toils under the sun?” (verse 3). The world described here is the world after Genesis 3, where work has become toil and every generation returns to the dust. The Teacher doesn't yet answer his question. He shows the reader the weariness of a world that keeps moving without arriving, and then introduces himself as the man best placed to search for an answer, a king with every resource and a mind full of wisdom.
historical:
The book's opening links the Teacher with David's line and with Jerusalem, and verse 12 says he was king over Israel. Tradition identified him with Solomon, David's son, who reigned in the tenth century BC and was famed for wisdom (1 Kings 4). The book never uses Solomon's name, though, and many interpreters think the author takes on a Solomon-like royal role for the opening chapters as a way to test life at its most privileged. Verse 16, where the Teacher claims to surpass all who were over Jerusalem before him, is often cited in this debate, since only David had reigned there as an Israelite king before Solomon; others note that Jerusalem had rulers before David as well.

The book's date is also debated. Those who see Solomon as the author place it in the tenth century. Most modern scholars date it to the Persian or early Greek periods (roughly the fifth to third centuries BC), based on its late Hebrew style. The chapter itself gives no historical events to settle the question.
cultural:
Ancient Near Eastern kings often left inscriptions boasting of their building projects, wealth, and wisdom, meant to secure a lasting name. The Teacher's claim of unmatched wisdom in verse 16 sounds like such royal self-praise, but verse 11 has already undercut it: there is no remembrance of those who came before, and those yet to come will not be remembered. The hope of every king who carved his name in stone is quietly dismissed.

The images of verses 4 to 7 come from the natural world as ancient people experienced it. The sun was pictured as hurrying back each night to its place of rising. The wind swirled and returned. Rivers ran into the sea without filling it, and people understood that their waters somehow returned to their sources. To a modern reader these describe the water cycle and the rotation of the earth; to the Teacher they are images of tireless motion that never achieves anything new.
literary: The chapter has three parts. Verses 1 and 2 are a title and motto spoken by a narrator who refers to the Teacher in the third person (“says the Teacher”), the first sign of the frame that returns at the book's end (12:8-14). Verses 3 to 11 are a poem whose rhythm imitates what it describes: going and coming, rising and setting, round and round. Verses 12 to 18 shift to the Teacher's first-person report, a form sometimes compared to royal autobiographies. Key phrases that will recur throughout the book appear here for the first time: under the sun, futile, a pursuit of the wind, and gain. The chapter ends with a two-line proverb (verse 18) that turns the value of wisdom upside down.

outline.t: Title and motto: everything is futile
The endless cycles: nothing new, nothing remembered

doctrines.note: The chapter describes life in a world marked by the fall: toil without lasting gain, generations that pass, and a heavy burden laid on humanity (verse 13). What is crooked cannot be straightened (verse 15), and human effort cannot repair what is broken.

Wisdom is the Teacher's instrument of search, and he has more of it than anyone. Yet it brings sorrow rather than peace (verse 18). The chapter begins the book's honest exploration of wisdom's limits.
The created world of sun, wind, and water keeps its steady order. The Teacher doesn't deny that order; he laments that its endless repetition offers humans no lasting gain.

words.note: Hevel, the key word of Ecclesiastes, translated futile or futility in the BSB. Its basic meaning is breath or vapor. Readers take it in several ways: as meaninglessness or emptiness (the NIV's meaningless, the KJV's vanity), as transience (life is a passing breath), or as enigma or absurdity (what can't be grasped or explained). The phrase futility of futilities is a Hebrew superlative, like holy of holies: the most futile thing of all.

Qoheleth, the Teacher. The word comes from a verb meaning to gather or assemble, so it may mean one who gathers people (a teacher or preacher) or one who collects wisdom. Its form is feminine, which may indicate an office or title rather than a personal name. The Greek translation rendered it Ekklesiastes, from which the book takes its English name.

Yitron, gain, advantage, or profit, a word found in the Old Testament only in Ecclesiastes. It is a commercial term: what is left over after the books are balanced. The Teacher's question in verse 3 asks what surplus life leaves when all the toil is counted.

Reut, a pursuit or longing. The phrase a pursuit of the wind (reut ruach) may mean chasing the wind or feeding on the wind. Either way, it describes effort spent on something that can't be caught or held.

christ: The New Testament takes up the language of this chapter. Paul says in Romans 8 that the creation was subjected to futility, using the Greek word that translated hevel in the ancient Greek version of Ecclesiastes, and he adds that it was subjected in hope, waiting to be set free. The Teacher's weary conviction that there is nothing new under the sun is answered, in Christian faith, by the resurrection of Jesus, which the New Testament describes as the beginning of a new creation. The link is not that Ecclesiastes predicts Christ, but that it names honestly the condition from which the gospel promises deliverance.

hard.q: Is the Bible saying that life is meaningless?
hard.a:
Read on its own, verse 2 can sound like despair: everything is futile. But the key word, hevel, has a range of meanings. Some interpreters do take it as meaningless or empty, and they read the Teacher's words as an honest portrait of life without God that the book's frame then corrects. Others read hevel as transience: life is a breath, brief and fragile, not worthless but passing. Still others take it as enigma: life can't be figured out or mastered.

The phrase under the sun also matters. The Teacher is describing life as seen from within the world's own resources, and the book's frame narrator will close by pointing to the fear of God and his coming judgment (12:13-14). Most readers agree that the Bible is not saying that God's world or human life has no worth; it is saying that nothing under the sun can deliver the lasting gain we seek from it.

questions: The Teacher asks what a person gains from all his toil. How would you answer that question about your own work?
Verse 11 says no one is remembered. How does that affect the way you think about legacy and reputation?
Why do you think verse 18 says that more wisdom brings more sorrow? Have you found that to be true?
